correctness.rationale: Exact renewal conditioning proves Eq. (1); killed OU backward equations prove splitting and negative-side mean; the scaled negative mean has an integrable linear majorant under finite-mean search clocks. Uniform integrability of Brownian motion stopped at the finite-mean search cutoff proves A=Lq0, canceling all reset-law dependence. Positive k has finite mean and k=0 infinite mean. The accompanying independently integrated verification program passed 59 deterministic assertion groups. The theorem is an analytic result, not an inference from those tests.

originality.rationale: The return renewal formula and boundary splitting are established prior art, expressly excluded. The assessed contribution is a quantified all-integrable-clock weak-harmonic-confinement amplitude, whose exact reset-law cancellation requires comparing singular OU return time against stopped Brownian search success. Full accessible primary-text comparisons and scoped scientific searches did not identify that exact theorem. Generic renewal implications and the uninspected precursor full texts remain residual priority risks, so this is a provisional self-review, not independent certification.
residual_risks: The 2024 and 2025 Biswas et al. precursor abstracts were inspected and arXiv HTML was unavailable; their complete full texts were not independently read.
A broad renewal theorem combined with a standard OU first-passage asymptotic and martingale identity could implicitly cover the result; priority is not independently established.
Similarity search has incomplete recall, and a negative search cannot establish novelty.

value.rationale: The vanishing-return-trap regime is physically singular and permits infinite mean without confinement. The leading divergence has a measured time-scale coefficient independent of any specific reset rate or waiting-time law, despite different finite-k behavior. This is a structural prediction about experimental protocol robustness with a nontrivial conservation mechanism, rather than simply rerunning an established finite-k formula.
